Follow the change of scale: a landscape contains rocks, and the rock contains distinct mineral grains.
Trace boundaries between crystals. Interlocking growth differs from fragments deposited together.
Identify separate fragments and the material between them. A clast can be a mineral grain or a piece of rock.
Use scratch resistance, not appearance. The ranks are not equal steps of absolute hardness.
Follow the weaker bonds and the repeated parallel planes. Count directions, not the number of visible steps.
Compare irregular or curved fracture with repeated planar cleavage. Broken does not automatically mean cleaved.
Compare the angles between the two sets of planes, not the outline of one crystal.
A cube and a rhombohedron both have three cleavage directions; the angles distinguish them.
Locate one silicon and four oxygens. This is the building block, not the formula of every silicate mineral.
Shared oxygen atoms link tetrahedra. Follow the links before naming chains, sheets, or frameworks.
Separate tetrahedra are held together by other ions. Distinguish isolated units from linked chains.
Electron transfer leaves opposite charges that attract. This differs from sharing a pair of electrons.
Electrons are shared across many atoms rather than confined to a single atom pair.
Carbon atoms form a strongly bonded three-dimensional structure. Compare this with graphite's sheets.
Connect the carbonate group with calcite. Calcite's acid reaction tests chemistry, not hardness.
Read composition across and grain size down. Follow mineral bands; color alone does not name a rock.
Identify the light minerals and visible interlocking crystals. Granite and rhyolite share a broad composition, not a grain size.
Identify coarse visible crystals, then compare with the fine-grained andesite image.
Notice the fine groundmass and vesicles. Basalt and gabbro share mafic composition but differ in grain size.
Look for the olivine-rich assemblage toward the low-silica end of the chart. Ultramafic is a composition category.
More time for crystal growth generally allows larger crystals. Separate cooling rate from magma composition.
The rock may be crystalline even when individual crystals are too small to see without magnification.
Find the larger early crystals and the finer groundmass. Explain the two growth stages, not merely the two sizes.
Look for the mix of ash and larger fragments. Fragmental texture differs from interlocking crystal growth.
Identify the very large interlocking crystals; this texture is different from gas-bubble cavities.
Read each axis. The geothermal gradient describes Earth's temperature profile, not the melting boundary.
Locate temperature, pressure, and the melting boundary before interpreting a point on the graph.
Follow a temperature increase at a given pressure across the melting boundary.
Follow decreasing pressure as hot rock rises. Melting does not require adding heat along this path.
Water lowers the melting temperature. Distinguish moving the melting boundary from heating the rock.
Viscous magma piles up; more fluid magma spreads out. Temperature, composition, and crystal content affect resistance to flow.
Compare upward movement through fractures with the trapping of magma at depth. Buoyancy and resistance to flow are different ideas.
Crystals obstruct flow. Compare a crystal-rich magma with one containing fewer crystals.
Read downward from higher to lower temperature. Contrast the discontinuous mineral sequence with changing plagioclase composition.
Partial melting need not produce a melt with the same composition as the original bulk rock.
Separating early crystals removes their chemical ingredients from the remaining liquid.
Country-rock material enters and may melt into the magma. Compare this process with mixing two magmas.
Connect rising mantle and lower pressure to decompression melting. Detailed lecture coverage of this section is not established.
Track water released from the descending slab into the overlying mantle. The mechanism is not simply frictional melting.
Identify a sheet that cuts across the host layers. Its relationship to layering defines it.
Identify an intrusion parallel to host layers. Parallel versus cross-cutting matters more than horizontal versus vertical.
Trace the domed layers above magma injected between layers.
Cooling contraction produces fractures. These columns are not individual mineral crystals.
Strong bonds lie within sheets; weaker bonds between sheets allow sliding. Diamond and graphite have the same element but different structures.
Locate shared electrons between atoms. Sharing differs from electron transfer followed by electrical attraction.
The finer groundmass distinguishes andesite from diorite. Larger phenocrysts may occur within that groundmass.
Identify the visible interlocking crystals. Compare grain size with basalt, not just darkness.
The smooth glassy appearance records a lack of crystal growth. Dark color does not by itself mean mafic composition.
The vesicles are former gas bubbles. Distinguish these holes from crystals and from fragments.
Compare the two incoming magmas and the combined magma. This differs from assimilating solid wall rock.
